faults.evidence: Arrian 1.7.5 (content/alexander-the-great/.references/archive.org-download-theanabasisofale46976gut-46976-0.txt.txt, line 1238): "He therefore led his army through Eordaea and Elimiotis and along the peaks of Stymphaea and Paravaea, and on the seventh day arrived at Pelina in Thessaly". Bosworth, Commentary on 1.7.5 (archive.org-History-20of-20Alexander-3B-20Volume-20I-20Books-20I-III-20-20A.-20B.-20Bosworth-djvu.txt.txt, line 5308): "he took the road through the pass of Siatista, leading to the headwaters of the Haliacmon, the heart of ancient Elimiotis. From there his route took him to Grévena, which is certainly located near the eastern border of Tymphaea ... From Grévena Alexander could have taken a direct route to the valley of the upper Peneus". Capture: .cache/scratch/020-map-auditor/shots/fall-of-thebes.png
faults.action: Points that take the march from Eordaea through the pass of Siatista (about 40.26 N 21.55 E) into Elimiotis, to Grevena (about 40.08 N 21.43 E) on the eastern border of Tymphaea, and down to the upper Peneus by Kalabaka (about 39.70 N 21.63 E) before Tricca, as Bosworth's Commentary reads Arrian 1.7.5. The route as drawn runs down by Kozani and Deskati, about 28 km east of Grevena. It never comes to the peaks of Tymphaea that Arrian names between Elimiotis and Pelinna. The plan's stations leave the place out too ("Pelium, Eordaea, Elimiotis, Peneus valley and Tricca, Pelinna"). Add Grevena to them in content/alexander-the-great/.plan/020-greece-secured/map.yaml.

faults.evidence: The note has Alexander go through the pass. The page's route follows Bosworth, Conquest and Empire ch. 2.II, "probably taking the inland route through Heracleia, Doris and the Cephisus valley rather than forcing the passes at Thermopylae", and runs about 10 km west of the marker. Arrian 1.7.5 holds for either road: "the Thebans did not learn that he had passed south of Thermopylae, until he was at Onchestus". The plan's `what` says the same: "Thebes does not know that Alexander is south of it". Capture: .cache/scratch/020-map-auditor/shots/fall-of-thebes.png
faults.action: The Thebans do not know Alexander is south of the pass, September 335 BC

faults.evidence: agents/pages.md, Zone families: "A marker's `color` names the family of the state that holds the place". The plan's map.yaml: "the allied people of the upper Strymon". Capture: .cache/scratch/020-map-auditor/shots/pelium.png (green flag on bare land)
faults.action: A family that does not say Macedon holds the land, such as `thracians` ("the Thracian peoples outside Macedon", the brief's family row). The marker stands on bare land, 8.3 km from thracians-340. The Agrianians had their own king, Langarus, and were allies, not subjects.

faults.evidence: The page's route follows Bosworth's inland road and runs west of the pass, and the marker note since 020-map-auditor-2 reads "The Thebans do not know Alexander is south of the pass". "Past" reads as through the pass. Arrian 1.7.5, as 020-map-auditor-2 quotes it: "the Thebans did not learn that he had passed south of Thermopylae, until he was at Onchestus". Capture: .cache/scratch/020-map-auditor/shots3/fall-of-thebes.png
faults.action: Thebes has no word that he is south of [Thermopylae](@thermopylae-335)

faults.evidence: research-020.md, 020.20: "the march into Greece, winter 336/335 BC". Capture: .cache/scratch/020-map-auditor/shots3/league-renewed.png (legend, last row)
faults.action: A season that agrees with the page's markers and its text: "winter 336–335 BC", as the notes of thermopylae-336 and corinth-336 give it and 020.20 dates the march ("winter 336/335 BC"). The legend reads "Alexander marches south, autumn 336 BC", and the text says "That winter he marches south".

faults.evidence: agents/text.md, "The text and the map agree": "each place it names is on the map". Capture: .cache/scratch/020-map-auditor/shots3/league-renewed.png
faults.action: The text names Athens twice for events of the page: it greets Philip's death with joy (Diodorus 17.3) and, alarmed as Alexander comes near, gives him greater honours than it gave Philip (Diodorus 17.4). The map shows no Athens. A note such as "Greets Philip's death with joy, then honours Alexander, winter 336–335 BC". The text links it once the marker is on the page.

faults.evidence: research-020.md, 020.3: "Crossing the river Nessus, they say he arrived at mount Haemus on the tenth day." Capture: .cache/scratch/020-map-auditor/shots3/the-danube.png
faults.action: The text says Alexander "crosses the Nessus" on the way from Amphipolis to the Haemus (020.3, Arrian 1.1.5), and the map has no Nessus. A label on the river where the route crosses it. Peuce, which the text also names, has no known site (names.md: "site unknown") and stays off the map.

faults.evidence: research-020.md, 020.9; names-020.md, Onchestus: "ruins near Haliartos, Boeotia, Greece". Capture: .cache/scratch/020-map-auditor/shots3/fall-of-thebes.png
faults.action: The text says the Thebans learn nothing of the march "until his whole army stands at Onchestus" (020.9, Arrian 1.7.5), and the map has no Onchestus. A marker near Haliartos, Boeotia (names.md), with a note such as "Alexander's army is here before Thebes hears of it, September 335 BC". Eordaea and Elimiotis, which the text also names, are regions the route crosses and have no label either; a label for each is optional.

faults.evidence: The text's "the army acclaims his son Alexander king" rests on 010.22, which cites Ellis alone for the army: "Antipater quickly presented him to the army, which acclaimed him king." (archive.org-mbridge-ancient-history-vol.-6-The-20Cambridge-20Ancient-20History-2C-20Vol.-206-djvu.txt.txt, Ellis, ch. 15). The page's rests_on lists 010.22, and its sources left the work out. The line takes the form the 010 pages give it.
faults.action:
- "N. G. L. Hammond and F. W. Walbank, A History of Macedonia III (1988), part one, ch. I."
  - "J. R. Ellis, \"Macedonian Hegemony Created\", The Cambridge Ancient History VI (2nd ed., 1994), ch. 15."

faults.evidence: The sentence keeps the words and the clause order of Bosworth, Conquest and Empire ch. 2.I (archive.org-onquest-20and-20Empire-20The-20Reign-20of-20Alexander-20the-20Great-20-281993-29-djvu.txt.txt, passages-020.md, 020.20): "the Thessalians attempted to block the main route through the vale of Tempe. The young king promptly circumvented their position, driving south along the coast and cutting steps in the face of Mt Ossa to bring his army into Thessaly to the rear of the enemy." The facts are found; the fault is the wording alone (step 5).
faults.action: The Thessalians bar the road into their country. Rather than force it, Alexander leads the army along the shore and has footholds hacked up a mountainside, and his men appear in Thessaly at the defenders' backs.

faults.evidence: The sentence retells the translator's words outside quotation marks, in his order. Arrian 1.1.4, tr. Chinnock (archive.org-download-theanabasisofale46976gut-46976-0.txt.txt, lines 835-840): "because he ascertained that these nations were meditating a change of policy; and at the same time, as they were lying on his frontier, he thought it inexpedient, when he was about to start on a campaign so far away from his own land, to leave them behind him without being entirely subjugated."
faults.action: Arrian gives his reason: the peoples of the northern frontier were restless, and Alexander wanted them beaten before he set off on a war far from Macedon.

faults.evidence: The list and the phrase follow Bosworth, Conquest and Empire ch. 2.II (archive.org-onquest-20and-20Empire-20The-20Reign-20of-20Alexander-20the-20Great-20-281993-29-djvu.txt.txt, passages-020.md, 020.4): "Using ships, log canoes and hides stuffed with chaff, he transported a substantial part of his forces across the Danube in a single night." The new wording rests on Arrian 1.3.6 and 1.4.2 (archive.org-download-theanabasisofale46976gut-46976-0.txt.txt, lines 979-988, 1008-1009): "He also filled with hay the hides which served them as tent-coverings, and collected from the country around all the boats made from single trunks of trees", and "in a single night".
faults.action: Overnight Alexander ferries 1,500 cavalry and 4,000 infantry to the far bank, some in the warships, others in dugouts gathered from the river folk or floating on leather tent covers packed with hay.
